extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of philosophy, history, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative principles, behavioral maxims, and practical rules embedded in Montaigne's Essays (early-modern philosophical reflections on human passions, public conduct, war, and death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do thy own work; know thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne cites the maxim (Plato/Cicero): 'Do thine own work, and know thyself.' One must know what one is and what is proper to oneself, avoid mistaking another man's work for one's own, love and improve oneself above all other things, refuse superfluous employments, and reject unprofitable thoughts and propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance stresses self-knowledge as foundational to right action: understanding oneself prevents taking on others' roles or pursuits that are unprofitable. Examples and authority: Plato and Cicero are invoked; wisdom is associated with acquiescing in the present rather than restless desire after future things. Anti-patterns: assuming other people's tasks or valuing office over virtue (e.g., revering princes regardless of merit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge and correct princes' reputations after their death
rubrics_metrics.description: The actions of princes ought to be examined after their decease; what justice could not inflict upon their persons may rightly be executed upon their reputations and estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues this practice is of singular advantage: it allows honest evaluation of rulers (distinguishing respect for office from esteem for virtue) and preserves useful examples for posterity. Anti-patterns: refusing to criticize a faulty prince out of private obligation, thereby privileging private right over public justice. Examples: Livy's observation on courtly flattery; Tacitus' anecdotes about Nero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral observances are consolations for the living, not succors for the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: The pomp of obsequies, care of funerals, and place of sepulture are comforts for the living rather than benefits to the dead; one should contemn the place of one's sepulture but not neglect it for one's friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends leaving funeral arrangements to the discretion of those who survive you and aligning them to custom and means. He condemns excessive vanity in arranging one's own obsequies (examples: men obsessed with specifying minute funeral details). He cites authorities (Cicero, Augustine, Socrates) and gives counterexamples of both extreme vanity and extreme parsimony (Marcus Emilius Lepidus). Practical rule: regulate funeral expense according to fortune; avoid obsessive prescriptiveness in one's final hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misdirected passions and fabricated objects of wrath
rubrics_metrics.description: When the soul lacks a proper object for its passions, it invents false and frivolous objects to expend itself upon; people often misattribute causes of misadventure so as to have something to quarrel with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne illustrates with many examples (people blaming food, gamblers swallowing cards, Xerxes whipping the sea, Cyrus attacking a river). Practical implication: be aware of the tendency to misplace blame or to forge petty enemies; check whether the object of anger or desire is legitimate. Anti-patterns: indulging in symbolic or impotent revenge (e.g., tearing hair as if baldness cures grief).

rubrics_metrics.name: A governor under siege should generally not go out personally to parley
rubrics_metrics.description: It has become a general rule among martial men that a governor of a place under siege ought not to go out in person to parley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: parleys are moments of high risk; the governor's personal sortie can compromise the defence, be exploited by the enemy, or be construed as despair. Exceptions: excusable if done so that safety and advantage remain on the governor's side (e.g., keeping within missile range of the walls, securing hostages first). Examples: approving Count Guido di Rangone's cautious behavior; disapproving Montmord and l'Assigni and others who exposed themselves. Anti-pattern: naive trust in the enemy's honour in the midst of siege operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parleys and negotiations during warfare are hazardous—do not trust until finally sealed
rubrics_metrics.description: During parleys and treaties of accommodation, one must be circumspect; confidence in an enemy is not excusable until the treaty is finally sealed, and even then victors may struggle to restrain their troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne provides many historical examples where parleys or conditional entries were followed by sack, massacre, or treachery (Mussidan, Phocaea, Capua, Genoa, Ligny). Practical rule: avoid admitting troops or relaxing guards until terms are irreversible; understand that handing the town over to a victorious army risks loss of discipline, avarice, and revenge. Note tension between moral rules of fair conduct and the pragmatic rules of war: sometimes advantage may justify stratagem, but risk is real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fair valor to stolen or treacherous victory (honour in warfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true victory is one obtained preserving one's faith and dignity; many authorities (Polybius, Chrysippus, Alexander) argue for avoiding stratagem in favour of open valour—victory ought to be won by courage rather than by deceit or foul play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents both sides: classical praise for fair combat (Alexander's refusal to use night-advantage) versus pragmatic acceptance that deceit may serve need. Guidance: valorous means confer honour; stratagem may win but is less praiseworthy. Examples: Achaians' abhorrence of double-dealing, Alexander's reply to Polyperchon, Chrysippus' maxim about running a race. Anti-patterns: celebrating treachery as superior to bravery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge actions primarily by intention; obligations are limited by ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral worth of actions is governed by intention: we are masters only of the will; obligations cannot bind us beyond what we are able to perform. Death may discharge some obligations, and making amends by will after death is often ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne discusses examples (Henry VII's posthumous command to kill the Duke of Suffolk; Count Egmont's wish to mount the scaffold first so death might free him of obligations) to show complexities: a will to do wrong cannot excuse premeditated infidelity; conversely, one who truly intended to keep a promise but lacked power may be absolved. Practical corollary: sincerity of will matters morally; attempting to correct injustices solely by testamentary acts is insufficient and perhaps hypocritical.
